etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English frogge, from Old English frogga, from Proto-West Germanic *froggō (“frog”). Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk fraug (“frog”), Old Norse frauki. Related also to English frosk (“frog”), frosh (“frog”), and frock (“frog”).

Possibly related to Saterland Frisian Poage (“frog”), German Low German Pogg, Pogge (“frog”).

definitions.definition: Any of a class of small tailless amphibians of the order Anura that typically hop.

quote.citation: 2008, Lich King, “Black Metal Sucks”, in Toxic Zombie Onslaught:
quote.text: Awesome leather armbands with spikes like two feet long / Hair is parted down the middle, frowning like a frog

definitions.definition: (music) The part of a violin bow (or that of other similar string instruments such as the viola, cello and contrabass) located at the end held by the player, to which the horsehair is attached.
(Cockney rhyming slang) Road. Shorter, more common form of frog and toad.
The depression in the upper face of a pressed or handmade clay brick.
An organ on the bottom of a horse’s hoof that assists in the circulation of blood.
(rail transport) The part of a railway switch or turnout where the running-rails cross (from the resemblance to the frog in a horse’s hoof).
(fishing) A type of fishing lure that resembles a frog.

quote.text: `What you need are frogs,' said the veteran. `Fish them at night. There's nothing like them on big cork floats.'

definitions.definition: (politics, slang, derogatory, Malaysia) Defector: politician who switches to a different political party.
To hunt or trap frogs.
(transitive, biology) To use a pronged plater to transfer (cells) to another plate.
(transitive, cooking) To spatchcock (a chicken).
(intransitive) To lie sprawled out like a frog; sploot.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From frog legs, stereotypical food of the French. Compare French rosbif (“English person”), from roast beef, corresponding term for the English, likewise based on stereotypical food; and Kraut for Germans.

definitions.definition: (offensive) A French person.

quote.citation: 1982 November 18, Antony Jay, Jonathan Lynn, “The Challenge”, in Yes, Minister, season 3, episode 2, spoken by Humphrey Appleby (Nigel Hawthorne):

definitions.definition: (Canada, offensive) A French-speaking person from Quebec.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Unknown. Possibly borrowed from Portuguese froco (“flock”), from Latin floccus (“flock”).

definitions.definition: A leather or fabric loop used to attach a sword or bayonet, or its scabbard, to a waist or shoulder belt.
An ornate fastener for clothing consisting of an oblong button (covered with netted thread), toggle, or knot, that fits through a loop.

quote.citation: 1844, Alexander Dumas, The Count of Monte Cristo:
quote.text: The visitor was about fifty-two years of age, dressed in one of the green surtouts, ornamented with black frogs, which have so long maintained their popularity all over Europe.

definitions.definition: A device used to secure stems in a floral arrangement, also called a flower frog or kenzan.
To ornament or fasten a coat, etc. with frogs.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Supposedly from ribbit (“sound made by a frog”) sounding similar to "rip it".

definitions.definition: (transitive) To unravel part of (a knitted garment), either to correct a mistake or to reclaim the thread or yarn.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Probably a minced oath alteration of fuck.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive, slang, mildly vulgar) To have sex with; fuck.
